title: Temperature
lead: Your hands cannot be trusted to say what is hot and what is cold, but a thermometer can, and temperature is defined to be what a thermometer measures. This section shows how many different physical properties can serve as a thermometer, lays the Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin scales side by side and gives the equations that convert between them, finds absolute zero where the pressure of every gas extrapolates to nothing, and explains why a thermometer left in contact with a body long enough reads that body's temperature, which is the idea of thermal equilibrium and the zeroth law of thermodynamics.
objectives: Convert temperatures between the Celsius, Fahrenheit, and Kelvin scales.
State the zeroth law of thermodynamics.
summary_html:
• Temperature is the quantity measured by a thermometer.
  • Temperature is related to the average kinetic energy of atoms and molecules in a system.
  • Absolute zero is the temperature at which there is no molecular motion.
  • There are three main temperature scales: Celsius, Fahrenheit, and Kelvin.
  • Temperatures on one scale can be converted to temperatures on another scale using the following equations: $\kTempF = \frac{9}{5}\kTempC + 32$, $\kTempC = \frac{5}{9}(\kTempF - 32)$, $\kTempK = \kTempC + 273.15$, $\kTempC = \kTempK - 273.15$.
  • Systems are in thermal equilibrium when they have the same temperature.
  • Thermal equilibrium occurs when two bodies are in contact with each other and can freely exchange energy.
  • The zeroth law of thermodynamics states that when two systems, A and B, are in thermal equilibrium with each other, and B is in thermal equilibrium with a third system, C, then A is also in thermal equilibrium with C.
notes: The four problems the book leaves unkeyed, frost damage at 28.0 °F in kelvins, the tungsten filament at 2900 K, Death Valley's 134 °F and the temperatures at which two scales read the same number, are left out.

exercises.prompt: Does the temperature of a body in internal thermal equilibrium depend on its size?

answer.solution: No, the system can be divided into smaller parts. Since no heat is flowing, each part is in equilibrium with the adjacent part, and according to the zeroth law, this means all parts are in equilibrium with each other and are at the same temperature. Quantities that are independent of size are called intensive quantities. Temperature is an intensive quantity.

exercises.prompt: What does it mean to say that two systems are in thermal equilibrium?

answer.solution: Two systems are in thermal equilibrium when they are in thermal contact, so that heat can pass between them, and no heat is flowing from either one to the other. Heat flows from the hotter body to the cooler one, so this happens exactly when the two have the same temperature, and once they are in equilibrium neither temperature changes any further. It is because of this that a thermometer can be trusted: left in contact with a body long enough, the thermometer comes into thermal equilibrium with it, and the temperature it registers, which is its own, is then also the body's.

exercises.prompt: Give an example of a physical property that varies with temperature and describe how it is used to measure temperature.

answer.solution: Any reproducible property that depends on temperature will do; the section names several. The volume of a liquid is the most familiar: in an alcohol thermometer the alcohol expands more than the glass around it as it warms, so it is forced up the narrow tube, and the length of the column, read against marks made at two known temperatures such as the freezing and boiling points of water, is the temperature. The same idea, that two metals expand by different amounts, makes a bimetallic strip curl by an amount that depends on temperature. Electrical resistance, the color of a liquid crystal film and the infrared radiation a body emits are three more, each read by an instrument that has been calibrated against known temperatures.

exercises.prompt: When a cold alcohol thermometer is placed in a hot liquid, the column of alcohol goes down slightly before going up. Explain why.

answer.solution: The thermometer reads the volume of the alcohol relative to the volume of the glass bulb that holds it. The hot liquid touches the glass first, so the bulb warms and expands before the heat has had time to reach the alcohol inside it. A larger bulb holds the same alcohol with room to spare, and the column drops a little. Only when the alcohol itself warms, and expands by more than the glass did, is it forced up the tube past where it started. The dip is small because glass expands much less than alcohol does, and it lasts only as long as it takes heat to cross the wall of the bulb.

exercises.prompt: If you add boiling water to a cup at room temperature, what would you expect the final equilibrium temperature of the unit to be? You will need to include the surroundings as part of the system. Consider the zeroth law of thermodynamics.

answer.solution: Start with the water and the cup alone. Heat flows from the boiling water into the cooler cup until the two are in thermal equilibrium at one temperature, which lies between 100 °C and room temperature and, since there is usually more water than cup, much nearer the water's. But the cup and the water are not isolated: both are in thermal contact with the air of the room, and heat keeps flowing from them into the surroundings until they are in equilibrium with the room as well. The room is so much larger than a cup of water that its own temperature barely changes. By the zeroth law, once the water is in equilibrium with the cup and the cup is in equilibrium with the room, the water is in equilibrium with the room too, and the final temperature of the whole unit is room temperature.

exercises.prompt: What is the Fahrenheit temperature of a person with a 39.0 °C fever?
To conserve energy, room temperatures are kept at 68.0 °F in the winter and 78.0 °F in the summer. What are these temperatures on the Celsius scale?

parts.hint: Fahrenheit to Celsius is $\kTempC = \frac{5}{9}(\kTempF - 32)$; subtract the 32 first, then take five ninths.
The same equation with 78.0 °F in place of 68.0 °F.

exercises.prompt: The surface temperature of the Sun is about 5750 K. What is this temperature on the Fahrenheit scale?

answer.hint: Go through Celsius: subtract 273.15 to get $\kTempC$, then $\kTempF = \frac{9}{5}\kTempC + 32$. Table 13.1 writes the two steps as one equation.

exercises.prompt: (a) Suppose a cold front blows into your locale and drops the temperature by 40.0 Fahrenheit degrees. How many degrees Celsius does the temperature decrease when there is a 40.0 °F decrease in temperature? (b) Show that any change in temperature in Fahrenheit degrees is nine-fifths the change in Celsius degrees.

answer.hint: A change of temperature has no 32 in it: the 32 is added to both temperatures and cancels when one is subtracted from the other, so only the factor of nine fifths remains.
